en: Having prostrated before the Lord of the wise, the God of gods, the Consort of Ramā, Saubhari composes this *Ekārthanāmamālā*,
which brings clarity to the mind.
Aḥ is Kṛṣṇa, Śaṅkara, Brahmā, Śakra, Soma, Anila, Anala,
Sūrya, Prāṇa, Yama, Kāla, Vasanta, and the blissful Praṇava.
Āḥ, Svayaṃbhū, Ribha, Vājī, Kheda, Śaṅkara,
Vāsava, Pārijāta, Sama, Prājña, Nivāsa, Caṇaka, and Suta.
He is desire (I), the immovable pillar, Indra, the sun, Varuṇa, the tree, the elephant;
he is the pure one, the glorious one, the unborn, the child, Viriñci, and the son of the Kṛttikās.
Īrīśvara would be an enemy; Karuṇa and Aruṇa would be men; Śaṅku would be childless, while Mukura and Nakula would have excellent offspring; Akula would be without a family.
Urgaurīpati, Ruḥ, Kāla, Setu, Nātha,
Parāyaṇa, Nārada, Arka, Anila, Pāśī, Mārkaṇḍeya, and Rāvaṇa.
Ūḥ, Pareta, Aṇḍaja, Tvaṣṭṛ, Vivasvān, Agnisārathi,
Vahni, Niśākara, Pūrṇa, Daridrī, and Saramādhipa.
Ṛ, Ṝ, Nṛti, Nala, Nāka, Khagarāja, Vāsuki, Śāla, the son of the father’s sister, Aditi, Diti, Umā, and Ramā.
Ṛ, niṣedha, bhava, pūṣan, varuṇa, amararāj, aja, karin, taru, nara, pāpman, vidvas, and ramāpati.
The letter *lṛ* signifies a barbarian, one of reddish complexion, a eunuch, a sinner, one who has been defeated,
one free from passion, a heretic, a lotus, and death.
The great-souled one, the god, the child, the king, the hymn, the narrative,
the fool, the penis, the anus, the armpit, the hair, and the man devoted to sin.
Eḥ, Kumāra, Asura, Arāti, Jñātīya, Ahita,
Uddhata, Ātmā, Śeṣa, Vivasvān, Kṛtārtha, Madhvari, and Śara.
Aiḥ is a cruel lord of the earth; Pūra is Māra, the immortal Asura;
Kulāla is Rādhara, the wise one; and Manda is a son, or else a man.
Orvedhā, Jña, Dhruva, Agastya, Garuḍa, Aka, Akṣaya, Asura,
Ākhu, Kāṇa, Mārjāra, Sādhu, Saṅga, and Parāśara.
Auḥ; a young dog, a man, a woman, the state of being, the subtle Prajāpati, the gross paramour, the possessor of arts, the happy one, Durgā, Rati, and the poet.
Aṃ is bliss, Kaśmala is suffering, Pūrṇa is that which has gone afar, and Vara is the best. Aḥ was previously mentioned among the Jinas; it is that which is praised by the servant of Viṣṇu.
Who is the Brāhmaṇa? Who is Mahī? Who is Durgā? Who is Sugrīva? Who is the Lord of Ramā? Then who is Ākhaṇḍala? Also, who is Sūrya? Who is Agni? Who is Vyādha? And who is Karṣaka?
An elephant, a horse, a serpent, a lover, a living being, an ant;
the earth, Lakṣmī, an enemy, anger, a man, a trumpet-flower tree, and a cow.
*Ku* is the earth, *kuca* (breast), *kūla* (bank), *kū* (a well), *kṛtyā* (a magical spell), and it is also remembered as *bhū* (the ground).
*Keḥ* means life-force, the sun, intoxication, and essence; *kaiḥ* is neuter and means one who is bowed down or pure.
Who? A dog; what kind of person? One who is dark-complexioned, withered, and consumed by grief; O bull among the Kurus! What? The head; what? Happiness, water, milk, sorrow, poison, and fear.
Ka is as previously mentioned; Kha is the Sun; Kha is the Earth (Mā), the Earth (Kṣmā), and Lakṣmī;
Khi is Kāma; Khī is Viṣṇu (Guda) and Brahmā (Dhātṛ); Khu is Fire; and Khū is Bṛhaspati.
*Khe* is breath; *khair* is existence; *bhrātā* is son; *khoḥ* is said to be lame (*khañja*).
*Khauḥ* is the lord of gods, fire, the Lord (*Īśa*), and the sun; *kham* is the sky and the sense organ (*indriya*).
Kha has been mentioned previously; now, Ga denotes Prīta, Bhava, and the supreme Śrīpati; Gā denotes Kṣmā, Ramā, and Gīr; Gi denotes Dhī; and Gī denotes Śrīmān and then Buddhimān.
Gīrvāṇī, gīḥ, surā, patnī, sudhā, guḥ, prāṇa, āsava;
guḥ, kānti, madana, bhīru, guḥ, setu, sakhā, ravi.
The word *gu* means excrement; *guru* means a dog; *gūḥ* means a sinner who deceives people;
*gaiḥ* means the Palāśa tree, the Aśoka tree, fire, the sun, a biped, and an elephant.
The word *go* signifies a thunderbolt, light, the earth, speech, water, heaven, a cow,
a goat, a bull, a direction, an eye, modesty, a preceptor, and Lakṣmī.

The syllable *ga* signifies the sense organ, Śrī, Rumā, musical instruments, refuge, and the excellent; the *ga* mentioned previously [is also included]. Now, the syllable *gha* signifies a son, fire, Pūṣan, a king, and an elephant.
Gha is Ramā, Śacī, Durgā, Bhūmi, Ghr̥ti, and Dharmaka;
Ghī is Kumāra and Amarācārya (Bṛhaspati); Ghu is Mūḍha, Akaruṇa, and Phaṇī (the Serpent).
Ghūḥ is the earth, ghūḥ is the lord of the gods; gudaḥ is the stainless Saṃkarṣaṇa;
gheḥ is Śaṅkha, Kurkura, and Kīla; ghaiḥ is Sūrya, the son of Saramā.
*Ghoḥ* is the sound *ghaḥ*; *surāvāsaḥ* (the abode of the gods) is *ghaṃ*; *pāpa* (evil) is called *gham*.
*Ghaḥ* has been explained previously; now, *ṅaḥ* is *prāṇaḥ* (vital breath), *turagaḥ* (horse), and *ṅā* is *dharā* (earth) and *ramā* (Lakṣmī).
From *ṅi* comes Bībhatsu and Nṛga; from *sūkṣma*; from *ṅī* comes Bhūpa and Kṛkalāsapa;
from *ṅu* comes Sūkara; then from *ṅū* comes Vyāghra; from *ṅe* comes Sūta; and from *ṅai* comes Parāśara.
The letter *ṅa* signifies a lion; *ṅauḥ* signifies the sun, Aruṇa, fire, and the moon;
*ṅam* signifies a canopy, happiness, the heart, clarified butter, water, poison, and milk.
I have previously mentioned Ca, Cu, Caraṇa, Arcirmukha, and Ravi;
Cā is Kadrū and Aditi, Kanyā; Ci is Pūṣan and Māṣa.
Cī, ma, ṣi, r, da, nti, pa, tnī, syā, ccuḥ, kā, lo, 'tha, pa, viḥ,
śa, raḥ, bhī, ruḥ, cū, rmā, rga, ṇo, 'pi, syāt, pa, kṣī, bhū, mi, ja, rā, ḍra, viḥ.
The letter *ce* denotes Kṛṣṇa, Arka, and Turāṣāṭ; the letter *cai* denotes Soma and the son of Vinatā;
the letter *co* denotes a heretic (*pākhaṇḍin*); and the letter *cou* denotes a cow, a bull, fire, and one who is haughty.
Ca signifies conduct, happiness, suffering, impurity, wandering, and water;
Ca was previously mentioned; then Cha is Soma, Chā is anger, and Chi is a potter.
*Chī* is the twenty-sixth vowel; *chuka* is the earth; *chūḥ* is the noose; *chaiḥ* is the abode of the gods;
*choḥ* is the full one, adorned; *chauḥ* is the wind; and *taru* is the tree.
The letter *cha* signifies smoke, the earth, one's own, a peak, a shore, a mouth, and a lineage;
*chaḥ* has been explained previously. Now, *ja* signifies a paramour, *jā* signifies the womb, and *jiḥ* signifies Sadāśiva.
Jīr is Jiṣṇu, Karuṇa, Yūkā, Jurviṣṇu, Jūr, and Kulālaja;
Jeḥ is Śunīja; then Jaiḥ is Pūṣan; and Joḥ is Vahni and Kamalāsana.
*Ja* is the unborn, the ageless, and the youth; *ja* is that which is born and silver as well.
*Ja* was previously mentioned; now, *jha* is the hand, *jhā* is the womb, and *jhi* is a digit (of the moon) and the monkey.
Jhīḥ is Karī; jhur is Bhṛgu; jhū is Dhruva; saṃgha is Amara; aruṇa is Jheḥ; carmakṛt is Bhava; soma is Roma; rāma is Jhaiḥ; and guru is Jhair.
*Jhoḥ* is known as Karṇa; *jhauḥ* is remembered as Nāka; *jhaṃ* is traditionally known as Maithuna.
*Jhaḥ* was mentioned previously, and now *ña* is Fire, while *ñā* is Old Age and also the Zodiakal Sign (Rāśi).
Ñiḥ is the sovereign emperor, the one aged in wisdom, and the fire; ñīḥ is the heretic who is fond of wine;
ñuḥ is the beautiful-eyed woman; ñūḥ is the well-dressed person; and ñeḥ is that which resembles gold.

With *ña* comes *kṛṣṇā*, with *ño* comes *palāśaḥ*, and with *ñau* comes *gauḥ*; *ñau* also denotes a heretic and a speaker of falsehood. *Ñam* refers to clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and is declared to be the supreme Brahman.
The previously mentioned *ña* is *prāgukta*; then *ṭa* is *plīha*, *mūtrakṛcchra*, and *pippala*.
*Ṭā* is *asūyā*; *ṭi* is *kareṇu*, *bhū*, *saramā*, and *dharādhara*.
From *ṭu* comes *kaṅkaṇa*; from *ṭū* come *cūḍa*, *nandā*, *svasā*, and *bhī*.
From *ṭe* comes *kāṇa*; from *ṭai* comes *dviḍandha*. From *ṭaiḥ* comes *prota*; from *ṭau* come *nabhas* and *haya*.
The letter *ṭa* signifies a preceptor, a disciple, one who is disciplined, a deity, and a bull;
likewise, it signifies an eye, an ear, a vessel, wandering, and death.
The letter *ṭa* has been explained previously; now, *ṭha* signifies son, knower, enemy of Madhu, talkative, void, and downpour; *ṭhā* signifies void and also the nose.
Ṭhiḥ is Kumāra; ṭīḥ is the enemy of the gods (Rāhu);
atha, ṭhuḥ is Kadamba, Yama, and Tvaṣṭṛ; and ṭhūḥ is both wisdom and fortitude.
The letter *ṭha* is the compound (*samāsa*), the expansion (*viryāsa*), and the totality (*samaṣṭi*) according to Gautama;
*ṭhaṃ* is knowledge, the void, the empty, the nectar, and the autumnal water.
*Ṭhaḥ* was mentioned previously; now *ḍaḥ* signifies "with wealth," *ḍā* means "the earth," *saramā*, and *ramā*;
*ḍiḥ* is Gaurī, *ḍī* is Śivā and Dhātrī; *ḍuḥ* is the moon, and *ḍūḥ* is the possessor of digits (the moon).
Ḍa is unrighteousness, ḍai is a bull, ḍaḥ is the ear, ḍo is a sinner, and ḍau is the lowest of men; ḍaḥ is a cow, ḍaḥ is a hand, ḍaḥ is a paramour, ḍaṃ is the eye, and likewise ḍaḥ is milk.
The letter *ḍa* was previously mentioned; now, *ḍha* signifies a dog, a cat, and likewise a donkey.
*Ḍhā* signifies the navel, *ḍhi* the anus, and *ḍhu* the penis, fire, and the fierce one.
Ḍhuḥ is a tortoise, ḍhūḥ a boar, and ḍhyālaḥ a serpent; ḍhūḥ is the breast, ḍheḥ is a young deer;
ḍhair is Māra, ḍhoḥ is a happy and excellent man; ḍhauḥ is the earth, and ḍha is excellent water.

The letter *ḍha* was mentioned previously; now follows *ṇa*: *ṇa* is a crocodile, *ṇā* is the navel, *ṇiḥ* is a wolf, *ṇaḥ* is ageless, *ṇīḥ* is heaven, *ṇuḥ* is a female elephant, *bhūrṇūḥ* is the Yamunā, and *saṭā* is old age.
Ṇa is the cat and viḍaṅga; ṇai is the jackal and harītakī;
ṇo is mustard seed (sarṣapa); then ṇau is māyā; and ṇam is said to be "vision" (darśana).
Then the well-attired one, the mouse, the bull,
the lord of Uma, the river, the ocean, the deer, and the lord of Rama emerged.
The syllable *tu* signifies a barbarian (*mleccha*), a thief, an elephant, a crocodile, a peacock, and the progenitor Diti;
*to* signifies the sun, an obstacle-maker, and a lord; *tau* signifies heaven, the earth, and likewise poison (*gara*).
The preceptor and the sacrificer [should offer] that grass and water;
then [there are] Taḥ, Prāgukta, Thaḥ, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and Vinatāsuta.
Thā is the Earth, Prabhā, Gaṅgā, as well as the Śirī, Godāvarī, and Yamunā;
thīḥ is the Ocean, Vraṇa, and Revā; thuḥ is the Witness (Sākṣin), and thūḥ is Parāśara.
Śuka spoke of the dharma of Gādhiputraka situated in the syllable *thervyāsa*;
with *thauḥ* is poison residing in a conch, whether the action be abundant or subtle.
Now, the previously mentioned *tha* is the giver (*dātā*); *da* is the female giver (*dātrī*), the auspicious earth (*dharaṇī*);
*di* is the female giver (*dānī*), the moon (*sudhānātha*); and *du* is the non-poor (*adaridra*), the hand (*kara*), and the lower one (*avara*).
*dūḥ* is remembered as sorrow, *deḥ* as wife, *daiḥ* as fish, and *daiḥ* as the bull Vāmana;
*doḥ* is arm, *hastau* are hands, *caraṇaḥ* is foot, *śiśnaḥ* is penis, *dauḥ* is heaven, *svargaḥ* is breath, and *prāṇaḥ* is son.
This gift is a refuge, an action that is auspicious, deficient yet blameless;
*da* was mentioned previously, while *dha* refers to the Creator, Viṣṇu, or the Son of the Mountain-Daughter (Śiva).
Dhā is the earth, Ramā, and Gaurī; Dhī is Dharma and the demon Vṛka;
Dhustanu, Dhūḥ, Kara, and Bhāra; Dheḥ is the bull, and Dhaiḥ is Rāvaṇa.
Dhau is Pāpī, Vṛṣaṇa, and Pūṣan; Dhau is Dharma, Earth, and Speech; Dhaṃ is wealth, shaking, giving, sustaining, action, and happiness.

The letter *dha* was mentioned previously; then *na*, meaning "non-existence" (*abhāva*), "not," "man," "heaviness," as well as "free from misfortune," "without passion," "human body," and "possessing a wife."
*Naḥ* means equal; *naiḥ* means a deer, fire, a boat, a ferryman, a man, and an immortal;
*naṃ* means an eye, collyrium, the ear, an instrument, a cause, and happiness;
*naḥ* has been explained previously; now, *paḥ* means a sinner, Pūṣan, and a son.
Pāparṇā, Piḥ, Pavitra, Agni, Pī, and Pipīlikā are recorded as synonyms.
Puḥ is "son," pūḥ is "city" and "body," peḥ is "embryo," paiḥ is "Gālava," poḥ is "grandson," pauḥ is "man" and "earth," paṃ is "pleasing," ṛṇaṃ is "debt," and payaḥ is "water."
The letter *pa* was previously mentioned; now, *pha* is Māgha; *phā* is the venomous serpent that hisses;
*phuḥ* is Kārtika; and *phūḥ* is the serpent Vāsava who has come for refuge.

*Pheḥ* is Phālguna, *phaiḥ* is Śaṅkha, *phoḥ* is Kāla, and *phauḥ* is Phaṇīśvara; *Garga*, *Droṇa*, *Raṇa*, and *Bāṇa* are also [associated with] *phaṃ*; and *pha* is remembered as both *phalgu* and *cāru*.
Pha was mentioned previously; now, bo is bimba, bā is remembered as the river Narmadā, bi is pūpa, bī is baṭu, pāda, be is sākṣin, bai is kaṇa, and raṇa.
*Boḥ* is life-force (*prāṇa*), *bauḥ* is the river Gaṅgā; *baṃ* is known as abundant strength (*bala-bahula*).
*Baḥ* was mentioned previously; now, *bhaḥ* is Soma, and *bhā* is beauty (*kānti*) and the goddess Indirā.
From *bhi* comes *patnībhiḥ* (with wives) and *bhītiḥ* (fear); *bhuḥ* is a serpent and *bhūḥ* is the earth;
from *jāta* comes *jātaḥ* (born) and from *bheḥ* comes *kāntiḥ* (beauty); *bhrūḥ* is the eyebrow, while *brāhmā*, *varuṇaḥ*, and *yamaḥ* [arise from *bha*].
The letter *bha* signifies a blow, as well as one who is timid; *boḥ* means Kaṃsa, and *bhau* means the Lord of Wealth (Kubera).
*Bham* refers to a lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), *bhayam* to fear, *brāhṛ* to nourishment, *bharaṇam* to supporting, and *payaḥ* to water.

*Bhaḥ* was previously mentioned; now *maḥ* signifies praise (*stoma*), Soma, Rāma, battle (*raṇa*), elephant (*gaja*), Jālandharī, pain (*vyathā*), Lakṣmī, mother (*mātā*), and month (*māsa*) is said to be denoted by *māḥ*.
Miḥ is Karṇa, mīḥ is the mighty-armed one, muḥ is his mother, mūḥ is the one of great strength;
meḥ is Sāraṅga, and maiḥ is Pūṣan, the excellent charioteer who is bowed down in reverence.
*Moḥ* is the wife; *mauḥ* is the abode of the gods; *maṃ* is auspiciousness; *malinaṃ* is impure flesh;
*maḥ* is as previously stated; and *yaḥ* is the heap, the Lord who is the son of Sudevī.
*Yā* is the womb, *yi* is battle, *yī* is an elephant, and *yū* is a charioteer;
*yuḥ* is a serpent, *yūḥ* is said to be a louse, *yeḥ* is a caravan, and *yaiḥ* is Vāsava (Indra).
The word *yoḥ* is a foot; *yauḥ* is a grain; *svargaḥ* is honey; *yaṃ* is effort; *karuṇam* is compassion; *madhu* is honey;
*yaḥ* is as previously mentioned; *atha raḥ* is desire; *vahniḥ* is fire; *sūryaḥ* is the sun; and *atha toyadhiḥ* is the ocean.
*Rā* is Lakṣmī; *rāḥ* is prosperity (*samṛddhi*); *riḥ* is camphor and Maheśvara;
*rīḥ* is Kāma, the king of men (Nala), and Agni; *ruḥ* is a deer; and *rūḥ* is Prajāpati.
*Reḥ* signifies weariness or awakening;
*raiḥ* denotes the color black; *ro* means anger; *rauḥ* signifies existence or heaven; *raṃ* signifies a jewel or wealth; and *rodanaṃ* signifies weeping.
The letter *ra* was mentioned previously; now follow *la*, *laca*, *lakṣmaṇa*, and *lalanā*.
*Li* is a serpent, *lī* is the earth, *lu* is the ground, *lū* is Rudra, and *lū* is Garuḍa and Aruṇa.
*La* is Lerlava, *laiḥ* is Kuśa, *rāmī* is Lormatsya, *lauḥ* is Prajāpati;
*laṃ* is Lakṣmaṇa, *sukhaṃ* is Nāma, *rakṣaḥ* is Śrotra, and *viṣam* is Vaca.
The letter *la* has been mentioned previously; now, *va* signifies a cripple, one who is happy, or a son of the gods (*tridaśaprasū*).
*Vi* denotes a bird, Garuḍa, the sun, the ocean, and the moon.
Vīḥ is Viṣṇu; vuḥ is a foot-soldier; vūḥ is said to be a multitude or an elephant;
veḥ is the Pārijāta tree; vaiḥ is the essence (sāra); voḥ is time (kāla); and vauḥ brings happiness.
*Vīḥ* is Viṣṇu; *vuḥ* is a foot-soldier; *vūḥ* is said to be a multitude or an elephant;
*veḥ* is the Pārijāta tree; *vaiḥ* is the essence (*sāra*); *voḥ* is time (*kāla*); and *vauḥ* brings happiness.
*Vaṃ* is happiness; *vasanaṃ* is clothing; *raktaṃ* is red; *vapuḥ* is the body; *vacanam* is speech; *āsuram* is demonic.
*Vaḥ* was mentioned previously; now *śaḥ* is Śambhu; *śā* is Gaurī, whose abode is the lotus.
*Śiḥ* is a bird; *śyatha* is good fortune; *śiśuḥ* is a child; *śuḥ* is a jackal;
*śākrkaraḥ* is immovable; *śūḥ* is a Śūdra; *śeḥ* is the Śirīṣa tree; *agaḥ* is a mountain; *śauḥ* is remembered as the king who slays the dull-witted.
Śa denotes the ear, sin, a child, Śaṅkha, auspiciousness, happiness, refuge, and the body;
the letter Śa has been explained previously. Now, Ṣa denotes the act of joining, fire, the sun, battle, and a particle.
*Ṣā* is a moat; *ṣī* is a she-wolf or a young dog; *ṣiḥ* is a conch shell, said to be circular;
*ṣīḥ* is a son; *ṣuḥ* is a hoof, a fullness, or Soma; and *ṣūḥ* is a Mleccha.

Ṣeḥ means "with a caravan," ṣaiḥ means "donkey," pāraḥ means "the other shore," ṣoḥ means "a dirty person," ṣauḥ means "bedstead," dharaṇī means "earth," buddhiḥ means "intellect," ṣaṃ means "grain," and dhāraṇam means "honey."
The previously mentioned *ṣaḥ* is the Sun; *saḥ* is Sūrya; *sā* is Sītā; *siḥ* is the immortal friend (Indra);
*sīḥ* is the happy one; *suḥ* is the axe; *rūḥ* is the sun; *rdharā* is the pregnant woman; and *narī* is the woman.
Seḥ is the essence; saiḥ is the parrot; śrvādaḥ is the barking [dog]; soḥ is Soma; sauḥ is the uterine brother (sahodara);
saṃ is happiness, refuge, that which is to be done, the primary, the course, and the excellent.
That which was previously mentioned is *ho*; *ha* is joy; *hiraṇyākṣa* is a thief;
*hā* is a Gandharva; *hiḥ* is a serpent; *hiḥ* is a man; and *harṣavat* is a deer.
Huḥ is remembered as King Nahuṣa; hūḥ is a sage (vipra); heiḥ is the performer of grace; hairhāsaḥ is the vocative; hoḥ is the vocative; haur is Viriñci and Ṣaḍānana.
*Haṃ* is stealing, *ha-ra-ṇaṃ* is taking away; *pūrṇaṃ* is radiant, *bhāsuraṃ* is shining, and *bharaṇaṃ* is supporting;
*bharam* is the previously mentioned *haḥ*, which is remembered as the defined characteristic of the supreme, eternal Brahman.
Kṣaḥ is patience, kṣā is the earth, kṣi is Sītā, kṣi is light, kṣī is the fire, kṣu is the base one,
kṣu is Vāsava, kṣū is the sun, and kṣūḥ is the most sinful destroyer.
From *kṣiḥ* comes the farmer; from *kṣaiḥ*, the fool; from *kṣoḥ*, the paramour; from *kṣuḥ*, the razor and the wound;
from *kṣauḥ*, the lame man and the upholder of the earth; from *kṣaṃ*, the field; and from *kṣaṃ*, water and honey.
The syllable *kṣaḥ* was previously mentioned; this verbal garland was composed by Saubhari and heard by Aṅgiras—may it purify the intellect of those who know it.
Thus ends the *Mātṛkānāmamālā* composed by the venerable Saubhari.
Having thoroughly examined all the lexicons of names, the eminent poet Amara proclaims this *Ekākṣaranāmamālikā*.
Aḥ is Kṛṣṇa; Āḥ is Svayaṃbhū; Iḥ is Kāma; Ī is Śrī;
Uḥ is Īśvara; Ū is Rakṣaṇa; and Ṛ and Ṝ are to be known as the Mother of the Devas and the Dānavas.
The syllable *la* is Devīsūlā, *rū* is Vārāhī, *vi* is Viṣṇu, and *raiḥ* is Śiva;
*oḥ* is Brahmā, *au* is Ananta, and the syllable *aṃ* is the supreme Śiva.
Who is in the sun that illuminates the self? Who is among wind, Yama, and fire? What is in the head, in supreme happiness? And what indeed is in the earth and in sound?

The word *kha* may be used in the senses of reproach and censure, as well as in inquiry and deliberation; it denotes a sense organ, one's own house, the sky, the mouth, emptiness, happiness, consciousness, and the sun.
The word *go* is known to mean a guest, a singer, a fragrant plant, a song, a leader, heaven, a direction, an animal, a thunderbolt, the earth, the moon, and water. It also means a mountain.
*Gha* is in *sughaṭīśa*, *ghā* in *kiṃkiṣyā*, and *ghu* in *dhvanau*;
*ṅaṃ* is in *mañjana*, *ṅo* in *vṛṣabha* and *ajina*, and *caḥ* is in *candra* and *cora*.
The syllable *ca* is used for the sun and the tortoise; *chaṃ* for the stainless; *ja* for the conqueror;
*ji* for victory, splendor, speech, the Piśācī language, and also for speed.
*Jha* is in the sun when it has set; *ña* is in the wind and in the gurgling sound of singing.
*Ṭaṃ* is in the earth and in the crow; *ṭha* is in sound, and *ṭha* is in Maheśvara.
*Caṃ* is in the void and in a loud sound; *ḍaṃ* is in the moon, in *maṅgala*, and in sound.
The prefix *ḍha* is used in the senses of fear and the absence of qualities; *ṇa*, however, is used in the sense of certainty.
The root *jñā* is used in the sense of knowing; *stṛ* and *kṛ* in the sense of spreading; *krīḍ* and *puñch* in the sense of playing; *day* again in the sense of compassion;
*bhī* and *trai* in the sense of fear and protection; *dham* in the sense of blowing; *dā* with the long vowel in the sense of wife; and *dā* with the short vowel in the sense of giving.
The root *dhā* means "binding"; *guhā* means "a cave"; *keśa* means "hair"; *dhātṛ* means "a creator"; *dhī* means "intellect" or "thought";
*dhūḥ* means "a burden," "trembling," or "anxiety"; *nau* means "a boat"; and *nara* means "man," "a kinsman," or "understanding."

The letter *n* occurs in the words *nistu* (in leading), *nu* (in praise), *nauḥ* (in a boat), *sūrye* (in the sun), *pastu* (in a protector), and *pāvane* (in purification); it also occurs in *jalayāne* (a water-vehicle). The letter *ph* occurs in *jhaṃjhā* (a storm) and *jala-phena* (water-foam).

*Bhāḥ* signifies splendor; *bhūḥ* denotes the world of Bhuvarloka; *bhīḥ* means fear; *maḥ* refers to Śiva, the Creator, and the Moon; *mā* signifies the head and measurement; *śrīḥ* is an indeclinable used for protection.

The syllable *muḥ* is used in the sense of a male, binding, and that which is in the wind (*mātariśvan*); *yaṃ* signifies fame; *yā* refers to a traveler, a bedstead (*khaṭvāṅga*), a vehicle, and Lakṣmī; and *ro* denotes sustenance (*dhṛti*).
*Tī* is used for intense fire, desire, wealth, gold, a cloud, and sound;
*rī* for delusion; *rū* for fear, the sun, a characteristic mark, Indra, and also movement.
*Laṃ* is used for oil (*taila*), *līḥ* for attachment (*śleṣa*), *lī* for fear (*bhaya*), and *vo* for Maheśvara;
*vaḥ* is the lord of the western direction, and *va* is also used in the sense of "like" (*iva*) or for Smara.
*Śam* means auspiciousness; *śā* means beauty; *śī* means lying down; *śu* refers to the moon;
*śaḥ* means clinging, again, the womb, liberation, and the invisible;
*sā* means Lakṣmī; *ho* means falling; *hu* means the hand; and *śūlini* means the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
The garland "śaṃ kṣetrarakṣasi" is said to have been approved by former masters.
Thus ends the *Ekākṣaranāmamālā*.
